preamble: Delateralization of the palatal lateral [ʎ] to the palatal glide [j] removes lateral airflow while keeping the palatal place of articulation. Best known as Spanish yeísmo, it independently completed itself in French (Old French fille [ˈfiʎə] > [fij], by about 1800), in Standard and eastern Hungarian (ly now pronounced like j), and in rural caipira Brazilian Portuguese (mulher > muié), making it one of the most frequent fates of /ʎ/ cross-linguistically.

examples.note: Most modern Spanish dialects merge /ʎ/ into /j/, so 'llano' and words with 'y' share the same onset.
The palatal lateral spelled -ill-/-il (also in 'œil' 'eye', 'travail' 'work') merged with /j/; the merger reached completion around the beginning of the 19th century.

In the standard language and eastern dialects ly lost its laterality and merged with j (the cluster lyj is pronounced [jː], e.g. 'folyjon' [fojːon] 'let it flow'); northern dialects preserve [ʎ], western dialects merged it with /l/.
Vocalization of lh to a glide is a stereotypical feature of rural caipira speech of São Paulo and neighbouring states, more frequent among older rural speakers.
